# LaTeX lint rules

Each rule has an ID used by diagnostics, `select`/`ignore`, and suppression comments.
These settings also apply to the [BibTeX rules](bib-linter-rules.md). See
[configuration](configuration.md#lint) for rule selection.

Each section states the rule's default. `tex-ls lint --fix` applies safe fixes;
`--unsafe-fixes` also permits changes to typeset output. Examples show diagnostics
and safe fixes generated by the linter.


## `abbreviation-spacing`

Report incorrect spacing after abbreviations and acronyms. Before a lowercase word, abbreviations such as `e.g.` need `\ ` to prevent sentence spacing. Before an uppercase word, a sentence ending in two or more capitals needs `\@` before its period. Initials, dotted acronyms, math, comments, and verbatim text are excluded. The rule is disabled under `\frenchspacing`. Both fixes require unsafe opt-in because they change typeset spacing.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A lowercase abbreviation followed by more text takes an interword space:

```tex
We tried several methods, e.g. gradient descent.
```

```text
warning: abbreviation-spacing
 --> example.tex:1:31
  |
1 | We tried several methods, e.g. gradient descent.
  |                               ^ `e.g.` is an abbreviation, not a sentence end; use an interword space `\ ` (`e.g.\ `) so TeX does not widen the gap
```

An acronym ending a sentence takes intersentence spacing:

```tex
The rover reached the USA. Then it stopped.
```

```text
warning: abbreviation-spacing
 --> example.tex:1:26
  |
1 | The rover reached the USA. Then it stopped.
  |                          ^ capital before sentence-ending punctuation suppresses intersentence spacing; use `\@` (`Word\@.`) to restore it
```

## `blank-line-in-keyval`

Report a blank line between entries in a closed, curated `key=value` argument. TeX treats the blank line as `\par`, which aborts the keyval processor. Blank lines inside a value's braces are allowed; unclosed groups receive parse diagnostics instead. The safe fix removes the blank line and preserves the following indentation.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A blank line separating two keys, which aborts the call:

```tex
\hypersetup{colorlinks=true,

linkcolor=blue}
```

```text
error: blank-line-in-keyval
 --> example.tex:1:29
  |
1 |   \hypersetup{colorlinks=true,
  |  _____________________________^
2 | |
3 | | linkcolor=blue}
  | |_^ blank line in `\hypersetup`'s key-value argument; the `\par` aborts the call
```

After applying the fix:

```tex
\hypersetup{colorlinks=true,
linkcolor=blue}
```

## `duplicate-label`

Report repeated label keys within one document's namespace, including shared source files. Definitions in mutually exclusive conditional branches are excluded. No fix is offered because either renaming or deleting a definition may be appropriate.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

The same key defined twice in one file:

```tex
\section{One}\label{sec:x}
\section{Two}\label{sec:x}
```

```text
warning: duplicate-label
 --> example.tex:2:14
  |
1 | \section{One}\label{sec:x}
  |                     ----- first definition of `sec:x`
2 | \section{Two}\label{sec:x}
  |              ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ label `sec:x` is defined more than once
```

## `deprecated-command`

Report the obsolete font switches `\bf`, `\it`, `\rm`, `\sf`, `\tt`, `\sc`, and `\sl`. The supported `\em` switch and locally redefined names are excluded. The fix replaces the command with its LaTeX declaration, such as `\bfseries`, but requires unsafe opt-in because font reset and math behavior differ. Commands used as references in forms such as `\let` or `\ifx` receive no fix.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

An obsolete two-letter font switch:

```tex
{\bf important}
```

```text
warning: deprecated-command
 --> example.tex:1:2
  |
1 | {\bf important}
  |  ^^^ `\bf` is deprecated; use `\bfseries`
```

## `deprecated-suppression-syntax`

Flag the retired `% tex-ls-ignore <rule>` and `% tex-ls-ignore-file [<rule>]` suppression spellings, which remain accepted for compatibility but are no longer documented. The Safe autofix rewrites only the family and verb to `% tex-ls-lint skip <rule>` or `% tex-ls-lint skip-file [<rule>]`; the selector and reason remain byte-for-byte unchanged, and the edit stays entirely inside a comment. This meta diagnostic is not silenced by the retired directive it reports; use `[lint].ignore` to disable the rule deliberately.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A retired suppression directive:

```tex
% tex-ls-ignore deprecated-command: legacy source
{\bf text}
```

```text
warning: deprecated-suppression-syntax
 --> example.tex:1:3
  |
1 | % tex-ls-ignore deprecated-command: legacy source
  |   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ retired suppression syntax; use `% tex-ls-lint skip` instead
```

After applying the fix:

```tex
% tex-ls-lint skip deprecated-command: legacy source
{\bf text}
```

## `missing-nonbreaking-space`

Report a space or single newline before a bare-number reference or bracketed citation, such as `Figure \ref{x}` or `see \cite{a}`. A tie keeps the reference with its preceding word. Self-describing references such as `\autoref` and textual citations such as `\textcite` are excluded. A same-line space has an unsafe fix to `~` because line breaking changes. A newline receives no fix; blank lines are not reported.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A plain space where a tie belongs before a cross-reference:

```tex
see Figure \ref{fig:plot}
```

```text
warning: missing-nonbreaking-space
 --> example.tex:1:11
  |
1 | see Figure \ref{fig:plot}
  |           ^ missing non-breaking space before `\ref`; use a tie `~` so the reference stays on the same line
```

## `obsolete-environment`

Flag math environments the community has superseded, naming the modern replacement in the message. The canonical case is `eqnarray`, which `amsmath` replaced with `align` decades ago (it mis-spaces relations and is a perennial l2tabu warning). The autofix renames the `\begin`/`\end` pair in place, leaving the body untouched, so it is an unsafe change requiring review of columns and package availability.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

The superseded `eqnarray` environment:

```tex
\begin{eqnarray}
  a &=& b
\end{eqnarray}
```

```text
warning: obsolete-environment
 --> example.tex:1:7
  |
1 | \begin{eqnarray}
  |       ^^^^^^^^^^ `eqnarray` is obsolete; use `align`
```

## `primitive-command`

Report plain-TeX primitives with LaTeX alternatives. Most replacements restructure arguments, such as `\over` becoming `\frac`, so no automatic fix is offered. tex-ls-equivalent replacements such as `\sb` to `_` and `\sp` to `^` have safe fixes. Locally redefined names are excluded, and commands referenced by `\let` or `\ifx` receive no fix.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A plain-TeX fraction primitive (report-only; the LaTeX form restructures its operands):

```tex
$a \over b$
```

```text
warning: primitive-command
 --> example.tex:1:4
  |
1 | $a \over b$
  |    ^^^^^ `\over` is a raw TeX primitive; use `\frac{...}{...}`
```

The plain-TeX subscript alias, carrying a safe swap to `_`:

```tex
$x\sb2$
```

```text
warning: primitive-command
 --> example.tex:1:3
  |
1 | $x\sb2$
  |   ^^^ `\sb` is a raw TeX primitive; use `_`
```

After applying the fix:

```tex
$x_2$
```

## `dollar-display-math`

Flag plain-TeX `$$...$$` display math. `$$` is a TeX primitive that bypasses `amsmath` spacing hooks and breaks `fleqn`/`\everydisplay`, so LaTeX steers users to `\[...\]`. The autofix swaps the delimiters in place and leaves the body untouched, so it parses and stays lossless; it is withheld when the display math is unclosed.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

Plain-TeX display math:

```tex
$$a + b = c$$
```

```text
warning: dollar-display-math
 --> example.tex:1:1
  |
1 | $$a + b = c$$
  | ^^ `$$…$$` is plain-TeX display math; use `\[…\]`
```

After applying the fix:

```tex
\[a + b = c\]
```

## `ellipsis`

Report three or more literal periods. In text, the safe fix uses `\dots` and separates it from a following letter. In math, the fix chooses `\cdots` beside an operator or relation and `\ldots` elsewhere. This choice requires unsafe opt-in because it changes the glyph placement. Comments and verbatim text are excluded.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

Literal dots in text:

```tex
See Chapter 2, 3, ... for details.
```

```text
warning: ellipsis
 --> example.tex:1:19
  |
1 | See Chapter 2, 3, ... for details.
  |                   ^^^ literal `...` ellipsis; use `\dots`
```

After applying the fix:

```tex
See Chapter 2, 3, \dots for details.
```

Literal dots in a math sum (an operator neighbor picks `\cdots`):

```tex
$a_1 + ... + a_n$
```

```text
warning: ellipsis
 --> example.tex:1:8
  |
1 | $a_1 + ... + a_n$
  |        ^^^ literal `...` ellipsis; use `\cdots` in math (`\ldots` for lists, `\cdots` for operator chains)
```

## `extra-alignment-tab`

Flags a row in a built-in `tabular`, `tabular*`, or `array` environment that consumes more columns than its column preamble declares. LaTeX cannot place the overflowing cell and reports an extra alignment tab. Short rows are valid and are not flagged. Custom column types and dynamic `\multicolumn` spans are left alone when their width cannot be established statically. No autofix is offered because either the row or the preamble may be wrong.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A row that exceeds the declared table width:

```tex
\begin{tabular}{ll}
  a & b & c \\
\end{tabular}
```

```text
error: extra-alignment-tab
 --> example.tex:2:9
  |
1 | \begin{tabular}{ll}
  |                 -- table preamble declares 2 columns
2 |   a & b & c \\
  |         ^ row uses at least 3 columns, but the table preamble declares 2
```

## `hard-coded-reference`

Report numbered references such as `Figure 3`, `Table~1`, or `Section 2`. Literal numbers do not update when the document changes. The rule requires a capitalized reference word followed by one space or tie and an Arabic number. It excludes plurals, lowercase forms, reference commands, citation locators, environment titles, item labels, math, comments, and verbatim text. No fix is offered because the target label is unknown.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A hard-coded figure number instead of a cross-reference:

```tex
See Figure 3 for the results.
```

```text
warning: hard-coded-reference
 --> example.tex:1:5
  |
1 | See Figure 3 for the results.
  |     ^^^^^^^^ hard-coded reference `Figure 3`; use `\ref`/`\cref` to a `\label` so the number stays in sync
```

Even tied with `~`, the number is still hard-coded:

```tex
Table~1 lists the parameters.
```

```text
warning: hard-coded-reference
 --> example.tex:1:1
  |
1 | Table~1 lists the parameters.
  | ^^^^^^^ hard-coded reference `Table~1`; use `\ref`/`\cref` to a `\label` so the number stays in sync
```

## `indented-docstrip-guard`

Flag a syntactically complete `%<…>` marker in a `.dtx` file when it is preceded only by horizontal whitespace on its physical line. Docstrip recognizes guards only at column zero, so an indented near match is an ordinary comment and does not select or delimit generated code. No autofix is offered because activating a guard can change generated files.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A docstrip guard indented by one space:

```tex
 %<*package>
\ProvidesPackage{example}
 %</package>
```

```text
warning: indented-docstrip-guard
 --> example.dtx:1:2
  |
1 |  %<*package>
  |  ^^^^^^^^^^^ docstrip guards are recognized only at column zero
warning: indented-docstrip-guard
 --> example.dtx:3:2
  |
3 |  %</package>
  |  ^^^^^^^^^^^ docstrip guards are recognized only at column zero
```

## `inert-suppression`

Report suppression directives that cannot act: `skip` without a following construct, `on` without `off`, or directives in `.dtx` documentation margins. Also report an unclosed `off`, which suppresses through the end of the file. No fix is offered because the intended boundary is unknown. Suppression comments cannot hide this finding; use `[lint].ignore` to disable it.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

An `on` directive with no matching open region does nothing:

```tex
% tex-ls-lint on deprecated-command
{\bf text}
```

```text
warning: inert-suppression
 --> example.tex:1:1
  |
1 | % tex-ls-lint on deprecated-command
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ `on` has no matching `off`, so this directive closes no region
```

## `invalid-macrocode-frame`

Flag a `.dtx` `macrocode` or `macrocode*` closing frame unless exactly four spaces separate its column-one `%` from `\end{…}`. The `doc` package scans for that literal physical delimiter, so a near match does not close the code chunk even though it looks like an ordinary environment to tex-ls. The safe autofix replaces only the malformed horizontal space with the required four spaces.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A `macrocode` closer with only three spaces after `%`:

```tex
%    \begin{macrocode}
\def\example{value}
%   \end{macrocode}
```

```text
error: invalid-macrocode-frame
 --> example.dtx:3:2
  |
3 | %   \end{macrocode}
  |  ^^^ `macrocode` closing frame requires exactly four spaces after `%`
```

After applying the fix:

```tex
%    \begin{macrocode}
\def\example{value}
%    \end{macrocode}
```

## `straight-quotes`

Report ASCII double quotes used for quotation. LaTeX uses two backticks to open a quotation and two apostrophes to close it. A paired quotation produces one finding and one fix; an unpaired quote produces its own finding. The fix infers direction from surrounding whitespace and delimiters, so it requires unsafe opt-in. Apostrophes, math, comments, verbatim text, TeX hex constants, and `\pdfmapline` font maps are excluded.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

Straight ASCII double quotes around a phrase:

```tex
He said "hello world" to me.
```

```text
warning: straight-quotes
 --> example.tex:1:9
  |
1 | He said "hello world" to me.
  |         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ straight double quotes; use `` `` `` (opening) and `''` (closing)
```

An opening quote after a parenthesis:

```tex
("quoted")
```

```text
warning: straight-quotes
 --> example.tex:1:2
  |
1 | ("quoted")
  |  ^^^^^^^^ straight double quotes; use `` `` `` (opening) and `''` (closing)
```

## `swallowed-space`

Report spaces that TeX discards after argumentless logo commands such as `\LaTeX`, `\TeX`, and `\BibTeX`. For example, `\LaTeX is` prints "LaTeXis". The rule applies only in text before an alphanumeric word. The fix inserts `{}` after the command and requires unsafe opt-in because it changes typeset output.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A logo swallows the following space, gluing it to the next word:

```tex
We used \LaTeX to typeset this.
```

```text
warning: swallowed-space
 --> example.tex:1:15
  |
1 | We used \LaTeX to typeset this.
  |               ^ `\LaTeX` swallows the following space; add `{}` (`\LaTeX{}`) or `\ ` so it prints
```

## `space-before-command`

Report a same-line space between a word and `\footnote`, `\footnotemark`, `\index`, or `\label`. Removing it requires unsafe opt-in because typeset spacing changes. Spaces after braces, at line starts, and inside math are excluded. For `\index` and `\label`, the fix also requires whitespace or paragraph end after the argument so it cannot join surrounding words.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A space before a footnote sets a spurious space before the mark:

```tex
This is important \footnote{See the appendix.}
```

```text
warning: space-before-command
 --> example.tex:1:18
  |
1 | This is important \footnote{See the appendix.}
  |                  ^ spurious space before `\footnote`; delete it so no stray space is typeset before the command
```

## `dash-length`

Report incorrect dash lengths in text. Numeric ranges such as `5-10` receive an unsafe fix to `5--10`. An en dash between words receives no fix because the intended dash is ambiguous; names with an uppercase letter on either side are excluded. The rule checks only words containing one internal dash run. It skips dates with several dashes, ISBNs, spaced dashes, flags, column specifications, label/citation keys, Beamer overlays, math, comments, and verbatim text.

This rule is **disabled by default**; enable it with `select`.

A hyphen where a number range wants an en dash:

```tex
See pages 5-10 for the proof.
```

```text
warning: dash-length
 --> example.tex:1:12
  |
1 | See pages 5-10 for the proof.
  |            ^ hyphen between numbers; use an en dash `--` for a number range
```

An en dash between words (ambiguous, so reported without a fix):

```tex
A well--known result.
```

```text
warning: dash-length
 --> example.tex:1:7
  |
1 | A well--known result.
  |       ^^ en dash `--` between words; use a hyphen `-` for a compound or an em dash `---` for a break
```

## `times-variable`

Report a lowercase `x` between two ASCII integers, such as `640x200`. The unsafe fix uses `\times` in math and `$\times$` in text. Ordinary words, spaced products, hexadecimal literals, and label/reference keys are excluded. Unsafe opt-in is required because the `x` could be an intended variable.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A literal `x` as a multiplication sign in text (fixed to `$\times$`):

```tex
A 640x200 pixel image.
```

```text
warning: times-variable
 --> example.tex:1:6
  |
1 | A 640x200 pixel image.
  |      ^ literal `x` as a multiplication sign between numbers; use `\times` for a cross
```

The same inside math mode (fixed to `\times`):

```tex
The grid is $640x200$ cells.
```

```text
warning: times-variable
 --> example.tex:1:17
  |
1 | The grid is $640x200$ cells.
  |                 ^ literal `x` as a multiplication sign between numbers; use `\times` for a cross
```

## `math-operator-name`

Report operator names such as `sin`, `cos`, `log`, and `lim` written without a backslash in math. Names must start a word and end at a word boundary; longer matches such as `sinh` take precedence. Subscripts, superscripts, text arguments, and unknown arguments are excluded. Adding the backslash requires unsafe opt-in because it changes glyphs and spacing, and the letters could represent a product.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A bare function name typesets as italic variables:

```tex
$sin x + cos x = 1$
```

```text
warning: math-operator-name
 --> example.tex:1:2
  |
1 | $sin x + cos x = 1$
  |  ^^^ bare `sin` in math typesets as italic variables; use `\sin`
warning: math-operator-name
 --> example.tex:1:10
  |
1 | $sin x + cos x = 1$
  |          ^^^ bare `cos` in math typesets as italic variables; use `\cos`
```

It fires through the glued `f(x)` form too:

```tex
The limit $lim(x)$ diverges.
```

```text
warning: math-operator-name
 --> example.tex:1:12
  |
1 | The limit $lim(x)$ diverges.
  |            ^^^ bare `lim` in math typesets as italic variables; use `\lim`
```

## `makeat-macro`

Report a command containing `@` outside a `\makeatletter` region. The lexer splits such a name into a command and following text, so TeX will not call the intended macro. Names inside the region and sentence-spacing `\@` are excluded. No fix is offered because the author must choose the region's boundaries.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

An internal `@` macro used without `\makeatletter`:

```tex
\my@command
```

```text
warning: makeat-macro
 --> example.tex:1:1
  |
1 | \my@command
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^ `\my@command` uses `@` in a macro name outside a `\makeatletter` region; `@` is not a letter here, so this reads as `\my` followed by the text `@command`
```

A leading-`@` macro (a `\@`-prefixed internal) outside a region:

```tex
\@ifstar{\StarredForm}{\PlainForm}
```

```text
warning: makeat-macro
 --> example.tex:1:1
  |
1 | \@ifstar{\StarredForm}{\PlainForm}
  | ^^^^^^^^ `\@ifstar` uses `@` in a macro name outside a `\makeatletter` region; `@` is not a letter here, so this reads as `\@` followed by the text `ifstar`
```

## `sectioning-level-jump`

Report a downward heading jump that skips a structural level, such as `\section` followed by `\subsubsection`. The hierarchy includes `\chapter` when the class supports it or the source uses it. Paragraph and subparagraph headings do not affect the comparison. Repeated levels and upward jumps are allowed. No fix is offered because the intended structure is unknown.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A heading that drops two levels at once (skipping `\subsection`):

```tex
\section{Introduction}
\subsubsection{Details}
```

```text
warning: sectioning-level-jump
 --> example.tex:2:1
  |
2 | \subsubsection{Details}
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ `\subsubsection` skips a sectioning level after `\section` (expected `\subsection`)
```

## `missing-required-argument`

Report missing required arguments from curated command signatures. Because TeX accepts single-token arguments such as `\frac12`, a finding requires a hard boundary: a closing group, math or environment boundary, alignment separator, line break, blank line, or end of file. Macro definitions, unknown-command arguments, standalone scope groups, aliases, and locally redefined commands are excluded. No fix can supply the missing content.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A fraction missing its denominator:

```tex
$\frac{1}$
```

```text
warning: missing-required-argument
 --> example.tex:1:2
  |
1 | $\frac{1}$
  |  ^^^^^ `\frac` is missing 1 of its 2 required arguments
```

A command left bare at the end of a group, with nothing to take:

```tex
\emph{see \textbf}
```

```text
warning: missing-required-argument
 --> example.tex:1:11
  |
1 | \emph{see \textbf}
  |           ^^^^^^^ `\textbf` is missing its required argument
```

## `undefined-ref`

Report references to labels absent from the document. The rule requires a rooted project with every include resolved to an analyzed file. It is inactive for stdin or without cross-file label resolution. No automatic fix is offered.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A reference to a label defined nowhere in the document:

```tex
\ref{sec:intro}
```

```text
warning: undefined-ref
 --> example.tex:1:1
  |
1 | \ref{sec:intro}
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ reference to undefined label `sec:intro`
```

## `undefined-citation`

Report citation keys absent from a document's bibliography. The rule requires a rooted project with every bibliography resource resolved to an analyzed file. Resource lookup respects `BIBINPUTS` and `TEXBIB`. A `\nocite{*}` marks entries as used but does not define explicit missing keys. Without cross-file citation resolution, the rule is inactive. No automatic fix is offered.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A citation of a key that matches no bibliography entry:

```tex
\cite{knuth:1984}
```

```text
warning: undefined-citation
 --> example.tex:1:1
  |
1 | \cite{knuth:1984}
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ citation of undefined key `knuth:1984`
```

## `unreferenced-label`

Report labels with no reference in the document. The rule requires a rooted project with every include resolved to an analyzed file. It is inactive for stdin or without cross-file label resolution. No fix is offered because the author may want to add a reference or remove the label.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A label that no `\ref`-family command ever targets:

```tex
\section{Intro}\label{sec:intro}
```

```text
warning: unreferenced-label
 --> example.tex:1:16
  |
1 | \section{Intro}\label{sec:intro}
  |                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ label `sec:intro` is never referenced
```

## `verbatim-trailing-text`

Report text after a verbatim environment's closing delimiter on the same line. TeX discards that text when it closes the environment. Trailing comments and ordinary environments are excluded. No fix is offered because the author must decide whether to move or remove the text.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

Text after `\end{verbatim}` is silently discarded by LaTeX:

```tex
\begin{verbatim}
sample
\end{verbatim} and more
```

```text
warning: verbatim-trailing-text
 --> example.tex:3:16
  |
3 | \end{verbatim} and more
  |                ^^^^^^^^ text after `\end{verbatim}` on the same line is silently discarded
```

## `duplicate-package`

Report repeated `\usepackage` or `\RequirePackage` loads in one file. Loads in mutually exclusive conditional branches are excluded. Macros such as `\ifthenelse` do not define recognized branches, and class loads are not checked. No fix is offered because removing a load may discard options.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

The same package loaded twice:

```tex
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{amsmath}
```

```text
warning: duplicate-package
 --> example.tex:2:1
  |
2 | \usepackage{amsmath}
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ package `amsmath` is loaded more than once
```

## `missing-provides`

Report a `.sty` file without `\ProvidesPackage` or a `.cls` file without `\ProvidesClass`. A declaration of the wrong kind does not satisfy the rule. Other file types are excluded. No fix is offered because the author must choose the declaration's placement, date, and version.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A package source with no self-identification (the docs are rendered against a `.sty` path):

```tex
\NeedsTeXFormat{LaTeX2e}
\RequirePackage{xcolor}
```

```text
warning: missing-provides
 --> example.sty:1:1
  |
1 | \NeedsTeXFormat{LaTeX2e}
  | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ package file lacks `\ProvidesPackage`
```

## `unknown-option`

Report package options absent from a loaded local package's `\DeclareOption` declarations. The rule skips installed packages, class options, and `key=value` options. A default handler, key-value processor, option forwarding, or `\input` makes the package's declared set incomplete and disables the check. No fix is offered because removing or renaming an option changes the requested behavior.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

With a sibling `mypkg.sty`:

```tex
\ProvidesPackage{mypkg}[2026/01/01 v1.0 Demo package]
\DeclareOption{draft}{}
\ProcessOptions\relax
```

Loading the sibling package with an option it never declares:

```tex
\usepackage[final]{mypkg}
```

```text
warning: unknown-option
 --> example.tex:1:13
  |
1 | \usepackage[final]{mypkg}
  |             ^^^^^ unknown option `final` for package `mypkg`
```

## `redundant-script-braces`

Report braces around a single-token subscript or superscript. The safe fix removes the braces unless adjacent text would change tokenization. For example, `x^{2}-3` and `y_{\alpha}b` stay braced because `2-3` and `\alphab` would become single tokens. Named math operators such as `\max` also retain braces because they cannot be unbraced script fields.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

Redundant braces around a single-token script argument:

```tex
$x^{2}$ and $y_{\alpha}$
```

```text
help: redundant-script-braces
 --> example.tex:1:4
  |
1 | $x^{2}$ and $y_{\alpha}$
  |    ^^^ redundant braces around a single-token script argument
help: redundant-script-braces
 --> example.tex:1:16
  |
1 | $x^{2}$ and $y_{\alpha}$
  |                ^^^^^^^^ redundant braces around a single-token script argument
```

After applying the fix:

```tex
$x^2$ and $y_\alpha$
```

## `unclosed-math-delimiter`

Report unmatched `$`, `\[`, `\(`, or `\left` openers in document prose when the parser retained them as plain tokens. Macro code can use these tokens literally, so the rule skips brace groups, optional arguments, expl3 regions, and `macrocode` bodies. No fix is offered because adding a closer and removing the opener are both possible corrections.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

An inline-math `$` with no matching `$`:

```tex
Let $x = 1 be the base case.
```

```text
warning: unclosed-math-delimiter
 --> example.tex:1:5
  |
1 | Let $x = 1 be the base case.
  |     ^ `$` has no matching `$` (unclosed inline math)
```

A display-math `\[` with no matching `\]`:

```tex
The bound \[ x + y follows immediately.
```

```text
warning: unclosed-math-delimiter
 --> example.tex:1:11
  |
1 | The bound \[ x + y follows immediately.
  |           ^^ `\[` has no matching `\]` (unclosed display math)
```

A `\left` with no matching `\right`:

```tex
$a + \left( b + c$
```

```text
warning: unclosed-math-delimiter
 --> example.tex:1:6
  |
1 | $a + \left( b + c$
  |      ^^^^^ `\left` has no matching `\right`
```

## `label-before-caption`

Report a `\label` before the caption or first numbered item that establishes its counter. Such a label captures the previous counter and can print the wrong reference number. The rule checks curated floats, `\captionof` containers, and the standard `enumerate` list. It skips labels nested in command arguments and ambiguous counter changes. The fix moves the label after the caption or item marker while preserving custom item labels and Beamer overlays. It requires unsafe opt-in because it changes reference output.

This rule is **enabled by default**.

A `\label` above its `\caption` picks up the section counter, not the figure number:

```tex
\begin{figure}
  \includegraphics{plot}
  \label{fig:plot}
  \caption{A plot.}
\end{figure}
```

```text
warning: label-before-caption
 --> example.tex:3:3
  |
3 |   \label{fig:plot}
  |   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ `\label` before the outer `\caption` in this `figure` does not capture the float number
```

A `\label` before the first `\item` has not seen the item counter step:

```tex
\begin{enumerate}
  \label{item:first}
  \item First
\end{enumerate}
```

```text
warning: label-before-caption
 --> example.tex:2:3
  |
2 |   \label{item:first}
  |   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ `\label` before the first `\item` in this `enumerate` does not capture the item number
```

A `\label` above `\captionof` in a minipage likewise precedes the explicit counter step:

```tex
\begin{minipage}{\textwidth}
  \label{fig:plot}
  \captionof{figure}{A plot.}
\end{minipage}
```

```text
warning: label-before-caption
 --> example.tex:2:3
  |
2 |   \label{fig:plot}
  |   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ `\label` before `\captionof` in this `minipage` does not capture the caption number
```

## Suppression

To suppress a rule at a single site, use a comment directive:

```tex
% tex-ls-lint skip deprecated-command: legacy code, leave as-is
{\bf here}
```

The verb carries the scope. `skip` covers the next construct, `off` and `on`
delimit a region, and `skip-file` covers the whole file wherever it sits:

```tex
% tex-ls-lint off deprecated-command: legacy chapter
{\bf here}
{\it and here}
% tex-ls-lint on deprecated-command
```

Naming the `<id>` is optional; leaving it out suppresses every rule over that
same span. The `: <reason>` tail is optional everywhere.

`% tex-ls skip` / `off` / `on` / `skip-file` do the same and turn off the
**formatter** at the same time; see [Formatting](../guide/formatting.md#turning-the-formatter-off)
for the layout-only `% tex-ls-format` spellings.

Parse diagnostics (rule id `parse`) are never suppressed by `select`/`ignore`.
